newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Defection boosts Drnovsek bid for Slovenia power.
newsitem.headline: Defection boosts Drnovsek bid for Slovenia power.

text.p: Janez Drnovsek looked set for a second term as Slovenia's prime minister on Wednesday after a defector from a rightwing party broke a two-month deadlock and appeared to give him a one-vote margin in parliament.
Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats won 25 seats of parliament's 90 seats in November's general election, which was Slovenia's second since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
During two months of negotiations, Drnovsek, who was president of Yugoslavia from 1989 to 1990, secured 20 votes from smaller parties, including the former communists.
But an absolute majority of 46 appeared to elude until Ciril Pucko defected from the Christian Democrats on Wednesday.
"Pucko has decided to support Drnovsek's candidacy. He has left the Christian Democrats," the leader of Drnovsek's Liberal Democrat parliamentary group, Tone Anderlic, told Reuters.
Parliamentary speaker Janez Podobnik immediately postponed the parliamentary vote, which had been due at 11 a.m. (1000 GMT).
Disagreements among the parties on procedure made it unclear whether the vote to be taken on Wednesday, officials said.
Pucko defended his decision to quit the Christian Democrats, saying Slovenia could not endure political deadlock.

"Slovenia at this time, 60 days after the elections, cannot afford further political stalemate," Pucko told Slovenian television. "We have economic and social problems that have to be solved not today, but yesterday."
"That is why I decided I would vote for Drnovsek. I will not join the Liberal Democrats but act as an independent deputy," he added.

His defection was certain to infuriate an alliance of three rightwing parties that had been confident of preventing Drnovsek from returning to power and of shifting Slovenian politics firmly to the right.

The alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, had won 45 seats in the election, and also needed one extra vote for an absolute majority.

Drnovsek, a committed pro-European, had crowned his four years in power by signing an association agreement with the European Union and vowed to reform Slovenia's economy, hoping got membership in 2001.

Slovenia, which developed into a stable democracy while other former Yugoslav republics were at war, won private assurances from Western governments that it could be a candidate for membership of NATO in its first expansion eastwards with the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland.

The so-called "Spring" alliance had been banking on People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik, 36, being called to form a government in what it believed was the likely outcome of Drnovsek losing the parliamentary vote.

Podobnik, a strong believer in the Roman Catholic Church and family values, had expressed caution over EU entry and called for guarantees of protection above all for Slovenian farmers, his party's support base.
